name: Smart Contracts and Executable Terms
title: Smart Contracts and Executable Terms
answer: Smart contracts and executable terms are contract provisions written in code so that performance, such as a payment or a transfer of a digital asset, happens automatically when defined conditions are met. They sit inside the contract lifecycle, from drafting and negotiation through execution and enforcement, and they can be used for simple tasks like releasing funds or for complex multi-step arrangements. The term smart contract is often used loosely, because the code is not a contract in the legal sense on its own, it is a mechanism that may sit alongside or inside a traditional agreement. Executable terms can also run on ordinary centralized systems, not only on distributed ledgers, when the parties want automation without a blockchain. The scope therefore covers the drafting of code, the legal wrapper around it, and the operational link between the two.

sections.body: Smart contracts and executable terms are contract provisions written in code so that performance, such as a payment or a transfer of a digital asset, happens automatically when defined conditions are met. They sit inside the contract lifecycle, from drafting and negotiation through execution and enforcement, and they can be used for simple tasks like releasing funds or for complex multi-step arrangements. The term smart contract is often used loosely, because the code is not a contract in the legal sense on its own, it is a mechanism that may sit alongside or inside a traditional agreement. Executable terms can also run on ordinary centralized systems, not only on distributed ledgers, when the parties want automation without a blockchain. The scope therefore covers the drafting of code, the legal wrapper around it, and the operational link between the two.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: What it runs on depends on where the executable terms live. On a public blockchain, the code runs on a distributed ledger such as Ethereum, where a virtual machine executes the contract logic and every node keeps a copy of the state. Developers write in languages such as Solidity, then compile and deploy the code to an address on the chain, paying a fee for computation and storage. For terms that do not need a public ledger, the same logic can run on a private database, a permissioned ledger, or an ordinary server, with an application programming interface connecting it to other systems. External data, such as a price or a delivery confirmation, usually enters through an oracle, which is a service that feeds off-chain information into the contract.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work usually starts with a natural language contract or a term sheet, which is then translated into code, often by a team that includes lawyers and developers. Drafters use templates, standard libraries, and testing frameworks to reduce errors, and they write unit tests that check each condition and outcome before deployment. Formal verification and third-party audits are common for high-value contracts, because a bug in the code can be difficult or impossible to fix after the contract is live. AI tools can assist by suggesting code from a clause, flagging inconsistencies between the legal text and the code, or generating test cases, but a human still reviews the logic and the legal effect. After deployment, the team monitors events, logs, and exceptions, and updates the legal agreement if the code needs to change.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area turn on who wrote the code, who controls the keys, and what happens when the code does something the legal text does not expect. Provenance matters because a smart contract may be assembled from libraries, templates, and generated code, so the origin and license of each part should be traceable. Risks include coding bugs, immutable errors that cannot be patched, ambiguous conditions, oracle failures, and uncertainty about which court or regulator has authority. Data protection and privacy rules still apply, even when the execution layer is a public ledger, and personal data should not be placed on chain without a lawful basis. Regulatory attention is growing, with many jurisdictions considering how automated and AI-assisted contracting fits within existing contract, consumer, and financial law.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward closer integration between natural language drafting and executable code, so that a single source of truth can produce both a legal agreement and a running program. Standard templates and shared libraries are likely to reduce the cost of writing and auditing smart contracts, while AI tools become better at translating clauses into code and explaining code back into plain language. Hybrid arrangements, where only part of a contract is automated and the rest remains in traditional text, will probably remain common because not every obligation can be reduced to a deterministic rule. Dispute resolution is also evolving, with arbitration clauses, on-chain mechanisms, and court rules beginning to address automated performance. The main open questions are how to handle change, how to allocate liability when code and text diverge, and how to keep the legal system's protections intact as more performance becomes machine-executed.
sections.heading: Where it is going
